explanation: In many homes, preparing and offering food is how families show love. When a patient refuses to eat, it can feel to the family like the patient is giving up or rejecting their care.

question: What does 'stock strength' mean when you look at a medicine label?

options.A: The amount of active drug in a specific unit of volume or weight
options.B: The expiration date of the manufactured pharmaceutical product
options.C: The maximum safe dose a human body can tolerate in a day
options.D: The total number of pills left inside the medicine bottle

explanation: Spot on! Stock strength simply tells you how concentrated the drug is in the package you're holding.

question: What does a holistic approach mean in palliative care?

options.A: Addressing physical, emotional, and spiritual needs together
options.B: Focusing exclusively on spiritual counseling
options.C: Relying entirely on herbal remedies and local roots
options.D: Treating only the physical pain of the patient

explanation: A holistic approach looks at the *whole* person—body, mind, and spirit. We don't just treat a sore body; we care for the heart and mind too!

question: Why is chemotherapy often given BEFORE surgery for osteosarcoma?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing post-op pain
options.B: To strengthen the soft outer layer of the bone cortex
options.C: To shrink the tumor and treat microscopic metastasis
options.D: To completely cure the cancer without needing surgery

explanation: Giving chemo first shrinks the main tumor mass so surgeons can save the limb, while also hunting down any sneaky invisible cancer cells floating around.

question: What is a key time-based rule for diagnosing obsessive-compulsive neurosis?

options.A: Behaviors must last continuously for at least five full years
options.B: The episodes must happen only once every month without fail
options.C: The rituals must occur strictly during morning hours upon waking
options.D: Symptoms must take up more than one hour daily or cause marked distress

explanation: Correct! For a formal diagnosis, these thoughts or rituals usually need to steal over an hour of the patient's day or cause serious distress.

question: What is the main benefit of using the 'teach-back' method during patient education?

options.A: It reduces the cost of buying medical equipment for the clinic
options.B: It measures the exact blood pressure of the client instantly
options.C: It eliminates the need for any further nursing documentation
options.D: It confirms whether the person truly understands the instructions

explanation: Brilliant! Asking patients to explain things back in their own words helps you catch and clear up any confusion before they leave.

question: Which common issue involves the compression of the median nerve in the wrist?

options.A: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
options.B: Lumbar Strain
options.C: Cervical Spondylosis
options.D: Rotator Cuff Tendonitis

explanation: Well done! Carpal tunnel happens when the median nerve gets squeezed as it passes through your wrist into your hand. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T3#GNS113_U3_T3_h3)

question: If a home care family is struggling financially and needs help finding community resources, who is the best professional to call?

options.A: Registered Dietitian
options.B: Wound Care Specialist
options.C: Medical Social Worker
options.D: Physical Therapist

explanation: Medical social workers are pros at navigating financial aid, government packages, and community support programs to help struggling families.

question: You are assessing a patient with a newly created AV fistula in their arm. What finding tells you it is open and working well?

options.A: A palpable thrill and audible bruit over the fistula site
options.B: Absence of any sound or vibration when listening with a stethoscope
options.C: A cool hand with weak pulses past the surgical site
options.D: A strong pulse with severe pain and redness in the fingers

explanation: You'll love listening for this in the ward! When arterial and venous blood rush together, it creates a gentle vibration (thrill) and a swishing sound (bruit) that confirms good blood flow.

question: Why does pickling food in an acidic solution stop it from spoiling?

options.A: Acid creates an environment that is too harsh for many pathogens
options.B: Acid removes all the protein content from the food item
options.C: Acid attracts beneficial molds that protect the food surface
options.D: Acid completely freezes the water molecules inside the food

explanation: Most harmful bacteria simply can't handle strong acid. Pickling creates an unfriendly zone where germs can't thrive.

question: In which dangerous condition should you NEVER give an anti-spasmodic medication?

options.A: Mild muscle fatigue
options.B: Seasonal allergies
options.C: Hypertension
options.D: Paralytic ileus

explanation: A paralytic ileus means the bowels have already stopped moving on their own. Giving an anti-spasmodic would slow things down even more, which can be disastrous!

question: What physical change directly leads to a loss of independence in degenerative muscle disorders?

options.A: Sudden increases in bone density
options.B: Rapid regeneration of nerve tissues
options.C: Permanent high blood pressure
options.D: Progressive muscle wasting and weakness

explanation: As muscle fibers waste away and weaken, patients gradually lose the physical strength needed to move and care for themselves. You've got this!

question: Why are dietary fats considered energy-dense?

options.A: They contain no carbon or hydrogen atoms
options.B: They convert directly into muscle without breakdown
options.C: They are digested much faster than carbs
options.D: They supply more than double the calories per gram compared to carbs or protein

explanation: You've got this! Fats give you nine calories per gram, while proteins and carbs only give four. That means fats pack much more energy into a smaller amount.

question: Why should nurses be quick to spot the difference between side effects and true adverse drug reactions?

options.A: To know which symptoms require immediate clinical action versus routine monitoring
options.B: To ensure the patient stops paying for their hospital admission
options.C: To calculate the exact lethal dose for the patient chart
options.D: To prevent the hospital pharmacy from purchasing the drug again

explanation: Catching harm early lets you protect your patient fast and report things properly. Brilliant nursing care in action!

question: What is the name of the system used in Nigerian health facilities for reporting priority diseases and public health events?

options.A: International Airline Passenger Registry
options.B: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR)
options.C: National Bank Financial Ledger
options.D: Global Air Traffic Control Network

explanation: Spot on! The IDSR framework is the backbone for tracking and reporting infectious diseases across Nigerian clinics. You're doing fantastic!

question: Why do clinicians love checking serum ferritin during a nutritional check-up?

options.A: It directly measures the body's stored iron reserves.
options.B: It calculates the total volume of circulating blood cells.
options.C: It tracks short-term protein intake over forty-eight hours.
options.D: It measures the exact amount of circulating vitamin C.

explanation: Ferritin gives you a sneak peek at how much iron the body has tucked away safely in reserve, long before actual anemia shows up.

question: How does strong teamwork across hospital departments act as a safety net for patients?

options.A: Multiple professionals cross-check information to catch mistakes early
options.B: It guarantees that doctors handle all tasks without nursing help
options.C: It removes all documentation requirements from the nursing shift
options.D: It ensures that patients never need to take any medications

explanation: Fantastic! When departments work closely together, staff watch out for each other and catch little errors before they ever reach the patient.

question: By about how much should a patient with symptomatic HIV who is losing weight increase their daily calories?

options.A: Up to 30 percent more calories
options.B: About 5 percent more calories
options.C: Double the normal daily intake
options.D: No change from normal intake

explanation: That's right! When the body is fighting active symptoms and dropping weight, it needs about 30% more energy to recover and maintain strength.

question: When do doctors usually order a polysomnography (sleep study) for a sleep complaint?

options.A: For every patient presenting with simple sleep-onset insomnia
options.B: As a mandatory first step before taking a patient history
options.C: When a secondary sleep disorder like sleep apnea is suspected
options.D: To confirm the diagnosis of acute situational stress

explanation: Standard insomnia doesn't require a sleep study. We order polysomnography when we need to rule out other medical conditions like sleep apnea or restless legs.

question: Which core nursing ethic requires you to keep a survivor's identity and story strictly secret?

options.A: Beneficence
options.B: Justice
options.C: Veracity
options.D: Confidentiality

explanation: Confidentiality protects patients from stigma and further danger by making sure their private health details never leak out without their consent.

question: What do we call a close call in the clinical area where a mistake almost happens?

options.A: A deliberate action taken to bypass hospital safety rules
options.B: An event that almost causes harm but is caught before reaching the patient
options.C: An unavoidable complication of a severe surgical procedure
options.D: An error that reaches the patient and causes mild pain

explanation: A near miss is your lucky break! It's when an error almost reaches the patient, but quick action or alertness stops it just in time.

question: Which type of transport needs cellular energy (ATP) to move nutrients against a concentration gradient?

options.A: Simple diffusion
options.B: Osmosis
options.C: Facilitated diffusion
options.D: Active transport

explanation: Spot on! When the body needs to push substances 'uphill' against a gradient, it has to spend energy (ATP)—hence the name active transport.

question: What is the main goal of teaching 'pacing' to a patient with fatigue?

options.A: To replace physical movement entirely with mental relaxation
options.B: To complete all daily chores twice as fast as before
options.C: To eliminate the need for any sleep during the night
options.D: To prevent total energy depletion by taking breaks before exhaustion hits

explanation: Brilliant! Pacing is all about working smarter, not harder. By resting *before* running completely out of gas, patients avoid crashing for days afterward.

question: Why do nurses strongly emphasize birth spacing during postnatal family planning counseling?

options.A: To guarantee that all children are born in the same calendar year
options.B: To ensure the family saves enough money for school fees
options.C: To prevent the mother from ever breastfeeding again
options.D: To allow the mother's body time to recover and reduce future pregnancy risks

explanation: Brilliant! Spacing pregnancies gives the mother's body, nutrition stores, and womb enough time to heal, leading to healthier moms and safer future babies.

question: Which type of lubricant must you use during a pelvic exam if a Pap smear is planned?

options.A: Petroleum-based jelly
options.B: Water-soluble lubricant
options.C: Surgical mineral oil
options.D: Silicone-based oil

explanation: You got it! Petroleum or silicone jellies can mess up cellular lab samples like Pap smears. Always stick to water-soluble products.

question: Why is it important for you as a nurse to understand female reproductive anatomy?

options.A: To prescribe hormonal contraceptives without a doctor
options.B: To diagnose sexually transmitted infections by sight alone
options.C: To accurately assess health problems and provide patient care
options.D: To perform surgical procedures independently in the clinic

explanation: Spot on! Knowing your anatomy helps you spot when something isn't quite right, chat easily with your patients, and guide them through different stages of life with confidence.

question: Who counts as a food handler in public health?

options.A: Only certified chefs working in large hotel kitchens
options.B: Health inspectors who visit restaurants once a year
options.C: Factory workers who manufacture food packaging materials
options.D: Anyone who touches food, equipment, or food contact surfaces

explanation: Anyone who comes into direct contact with food, cooking tools, or preparation surfaces during their work is considered a food handler. You've got this!

question: What often happens when healthcare team members communicate poorly with each other?

options.A: Better coordination of community support services
options.B: Medication errors and conflicting care instructions
options.C: Increased satisfaction among family caregivers
options.D: Faster recovery times for hospitalized patients

explanation: When health workers don't share updates, mistakes happen, and patients might get mixed-up advice or wrong treatments.

question: Why is a patient usually asked to lie flat after a lumbar puncture?

options.A: To help prevent a low-pressure spinal headache
options.B: To speed up the absorption of the local anesthetic
options.C: To keep the blood pressure from dropping too fast
options.D: To prevent the collection tubes from falling over

explanation: Correct! Lying flat reduces pull on the meninges where the needle went in, lowering the chance of a terrible headache.

question: What is a major risk when relying only on written charts during an audit?

options.A: Patients will refuse to take their prescribed hospital medications
options.B: Doctors will take over all the responsibilities of the nursing staff
options.C: Care might have been given but simply not documented by the nurse
options.D: Case notes might turn into digital files without any human input

explanation: Exactly! Heavy workloads on the ward sometimes mean a nurse performed a procedure wonderfully, but was simply too busy to write it down.

question: Why do some oral medications need to be given in much higher doses than IV (intravenous) medications?

options.A: To ensure the drug binds tightly to red blood cells instantly
options.B: To prevent the stomach acid from expanding the capsule size
options.C: To make up for drug lost to the first-pass effect in the liver
options.D: To speed up the rate of renal filtration in the kidneys

explanation: When you swallow a pill, the liver catches and breaks down a good chunk of it before it reaches anywhere else (the first-pass effect). So doctors prescribe a bit extra to make sure enough drug survives!

question: Which practice is legally and ethically required when disciplining a nurse?

options.A: Allowing other nurses to vote on the penalty
options.B: Discussing the issue openly with patients
options.C: Maintaining strict confidentiality of the details
options.D: Announcing the disciplinary action at staff meetings

explanation: Disciplinary records and meetings are private personnel matters that must never be shared publicly. [learn more](GST321_U1_T22#GST321_U1_T22_h7)

question: Why is spousal communication often encouraged in Nigerian family planning counselling?

options.A: Partner support helps improve long-term contraceptive adherence
options.B: Nigerian law prohibits women from buying drugs independently
options.C: Men are the only ones who experience contraceptive side effects
options.D: Husbands must legally sign all medical forms in public hospitals

explanation: When partners understand and support the chosen method, the client faces less household conflict and continues use more successfully. [learn more](GNS226_U6_T022#GNS226_U6_T022_h8)

question: What is the name of the temperature zone where bacteria grow and multiply the fastest?

options.C: 0°C to 4°C
options.D: 5°C to 60°C

explanation: The 'danger zone' is between 5°C and 60°C. In this warmth, bacteria can double in number in just twenty minutes!

question: How does disease surveillance differ from standard bedside nursing care?

options.A: Surveillance is only performed by doctors inside specialized laboratories
options.B: Surveillance deals exclusively with chronic genetic disorders
options.C: Surveillance requires advanced surgical skills instead of basic bedside observation
options.D: Surveillance focuses on population-level health trends rather than single patients

explanation: While bedside nursing cares for one patient at a time, surveillance looks at the big picture to protect entire communities. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: What is the main focus of occupational therapy in subacute care?

options.A: Helping patients perform daily self-care tasks like dressing and bathing
options.B: Managing complex intravenous medications and wound dressings
options.C: Assessing nutritional intake and feeding tube placement needs
options.D: Restoring walking ability and lower body muscle strength

explanation: You nailed it! Occupational therapy focuses on helping clients get back to doing everyday activities independently.

question: What makes a family 'vulnerable' in community nursing?

options.A: Living only in rural farming settlements
options.B: Always rejecting nursing advice
options.C: Lacking resources to handle daily stress and crises
options.D: Refusing to join community health programs

explanation: Spot on! Vulnerable families simply lack the money, social support, or physical resources needed to bounce back from life's everyday shocks. You've got this!

question: If someone has a family history of anxiety, what role does a major life stressor play?

options.A: It only affects physical heart rate and blood pressure
options.B: It can act as a trigger that activates the underlying condition
options.C: It completely erases any chance of developing symptoms
options.D: It replaces the need for biological evaluation entirely

explanation: Think of the genetic tendency as a loaded gun, and severe stress as the trigger that pulls it.

question: As a nurse, which non-clinical duty do you often perform in financed health systems?

options.A: Managing the national treasury accounts
options.B: Explaining insurance coverage and benefits to patients
options.C: Collecting taxes from local business owners
options.D: Setting the annual interest rates for community loans

explanation: Nurses are great educators! You will often help bridge the gap by explaining complex health programs in plain language patients can easily understand.

question: What happens when healthcare staff fail to follow isolation protocols consistently?

options.A: The patient's room stays cleaner longer
options.B: The hospital saves money on purchasing protective gear
options.C: Infections can spread rapidly to other patients and staff
options.D: Patients recover faster due to less medical disturbance

explanation: Inconsistent compliance breaks the safety barrier, allowing dangerous pathogens to escape the room and infect others. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h8)

question: A cook slices raw beef and immediately uses the same unwashed knife to cut fresh tomatoes. What just happened?

options.A: Improper freezing
options.B: Thermal abuse
options.C: Cross-contamination
options.D: Food adulteration

explanation: Correct! Using the same knife without washing it transfers bacteria directly from the raw meat into the fresh veggies.

question: Which factor makes a woman more likely to get vulval varicosities in her later pregnancies?

options.A: Early menarche
options.B: High dietary iron
options.C: Multiparity
options.D: First pregnancy

explanation: Multiparity just means having had multiple pregnancies! Each time, the pelvic veins stretch out a bit more, making them more prone to swelling in future pregnancies.

question: Why is tetanus considered infectious, but not strictly communicable?

options.A: It spreads through the air rather than direct contact.
options.B: It cannot be treated with any known medications.
options.C: It only affects animals and never human beings.
options.D: It enters the body from the environment and does not spread from person to person.

explanation: Think of it this way: tetanus spores live in the soil and get in through wounds. You cannot catch tetanus directly from a patient lying next to you in the ward!

question: Which type of research relies mostly on numbers and statistics?

options.A: Phenomenological research
options.B: Qualitative research
options.C: Ethnographic research
options.D: Quantitative research

explanation: You nailed it! Quantitative research deals with measurable variables and numbers to find clear patterns and test relationships. Think 'quant' for quantity and numbers! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h3)

question: Think of a theoretical framework as the backbone of a nursing study. What is its main job?

options.A: Providing funding for data collection and equipment
options.B: Serving as the structural foundation and guide for the study
options.C: Determining the exact sample size needed for the project
options.D: Writing the final reference list in the correct format

explanation: Spot on! Just like a physical building needs a strong frame to stand, a research study needs a theoretical framework to shape how it is designed and understood.

question: Why do we need to manage hospital waste carefully?

options.A: To maintain a pleasant smell throughout the hospital wards
options.B: To reduce the overall cost of hospital administrative duties
options.C: To ensure that all medical supplies are completely recycled
options.D: To prevent infections, toxic injuries, and sharp punctures

explanation: Hazardous waste carries germs and dangerous materials that can easily hurt patients, hospital staff, and the public if we aren't careful.

question: What is the purpose of the 'teach-back' method in home care?

options.A: Allowing the nurse to grade the family's cleaning skills
options.B: Checking if the patient or caregiver truly understands instructions
options.C: Testing the patient's ability to read a textbook out loud
options.D: Teaching the nurse how to use home appliances

explanation: Instead of asking 'Do you understand?', you ask them to explain the instructions back to you in their own words. It's a game-changer for safety!

question: Why does the actual amount of oxygen (FiO2) a patient receives from a nasal cannula vary from person to person?

options.A: Different hospitals calibrate their wall oxygen outlets to different pressures
options.B: It depends on the patient's breathing rate and depth, which mixes room air with the oxygen
options.C: Patients absorb oxygen at different speeds through their skin
options.D: The plastic tubing stretches or shrinks based on the room temperature

explanation: Because a nasal cannula is an open system, patients breathe in regular room air right along with the oxygen. How fast or deep they breathe changes the exact mix!

question: What do we call the basic grid system of rows and columns in Excel?

options.A: A word processor
options.B: A database table
options.C: A presentation slide
options.D: A spreadsheet

explanation: Excel is all about spreadsheets! The rows and columns give you a neat grid to organize and crunch numbers easily. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T8#GNS113_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why does eating a fatty meal trigger severe pain in someone with gallstones?

options.A: Stomach acid mixes with fat to create a toxic gas.
options.B: The liver swells instantly from eating too much oil.
options.C: The gallbladder contracts to release bile against blocked stones.
options.D: Fat directly irritates the lining of the stomach.

explanation: When fat hits the small intestine, your gallbladder squeezes to send out bile. If gallstones are blocking the path, that squeeze causes sharp pain!

question: Which assessment technique uses a stethoscope to listen to sounds inside the body?

options.A: Percussion
options.B: Inspection
options.C: Auscultation
options.D: Palpation

explanation: Auscultation is just the clinical word for listening! You use your stethoscope to tune into heartbeats, breathing sounds, and tummy rumbles.

question: What legal defense applies when a patient's own carelessness helped cause their injury?

options.A: Good Samaritan law
options.B: Assumption of risk
options.C: Statute of limitations
options.D: Comparative negligence

explanation: If the patient shares the blame for their own injury (like ignoring direct medical advice), this defense helps reduce or block the liability.

question: A nurse is getting the delivery room ready for an expected birth. What should be checked first?

options.A: Dimming all room lights to create a relaxing sleep environment
options.B: Staging extra visitor chairs around the bed for family members
options.C: Checking that emergency resuscitation equipment and oxytocin are ready
options.D: Ensuring the windows are wide open to maximize cool fresh air circulation

explanation: Always expect the unexpected in labour! Having your emergency tools and oxytocin ready means you can act lightning-fast if complications pop up.

question: Why does someone who has recovered from chickenpox almost never catch it a second time?

options.A: Red blood cells absorb and neutralize the viral particles in the blood
options.B: Innate physical barriers permanently change to block the virus from entering
options.C: Adaptive memory cells remain in the body to recognize the virus immediately
options.D: Stomach acid adapts to destroy the chickenpox virus on contact

explanation: Your body leaves behind 'memory cells' after an infection. If the chickenpox virus dares to show its face again, these memory cells recognize it instantly and crush it!

question: What is the main point of using motivational interviewing during nutrition counseling?

options.A: Testing the patient on their knowledge of food biochemistry
options.B: Allowing the nurse to firmly dictate strict rules for weight loss
options.C: Speeding up the clinical consultation to save hospital time
options.D: Helping patients resolve their ambivalence about changing eating habits

explanation: Spot on. Motivational interviewing helps patients work through their mixed feelings so they can find their own inner drive to change.

question: What is the main difference between congenital and acquired disabilities?

options.A: Acquired conditions never cause any emotional distress or grief
options.B: Congenital conditions are present from birth, while acquired ones happen later in life
options.C: Acquired conditions are always genetic and passed down in families
options.D: Congenital conditions only affect older adults in the community

explanation: You've got it! 'Congenital' means it's been there since birth, while 'acquired' means something happened later in life to change their physical abilities.

question: How does a 'just culture' respond when a nurse makes an honest, accidental error?

options.A: It requires the nurse to pay out-of-pocket for any hospital damages
options.B: It mandates immediate termination of employment to protect patients
options.C: It treats the error as a signal to examine and fix the underlying system
options.D: It ignores the incident completely to avoid creating paperwork

explanation: A just culture knows good nurses make mistakes. Instead of pointing fingers, it asks: 'How can we fix the system so this doesn't happen again?'

question: Why is early adolescent pregnancy so physically dangerous for a young girl?

options.A: Infants born to teenagers are immune to all childhood infections.
options.B: Her pelvic bones and reproductive system are still growing and physically immature.
options.C: Medical practitioners refuse to provide antenatal care to underage mothers.
options.D: Pregnant adolescents stop producing natural hormones required for gestation.

explanation: A young girl's body is simply not ready to carry and deliver a baby. An immature pelvis makes obstructed labor a major, life-threatening risk.

question: Why must a nurse stay at the bedside until the patient swallows all their medications?

options.A: To record the exact second the patient stops drinking water
options.B: To collect payment for the hospital prescription fees
options.C: To make sure the water cup is returned clean to the medication room
options.D: To confirm the patient actually takes the drugs and does not hide them

explanation: Staying at the bedside ensures compliance and safety, preventing patients from pocketing pills or missing doses. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: As a nurse researcher, why would you choose to use qualitative interviews?

options.A: To measure exact physiological vital signs over time
options.B: To explore deep human experiences and personal perspectives
options.C: To test new pharmaceutical drugs on large populations
options.D: To calculate statistical averages of hospital stays

explanation: You've got this! Qualitative interviews are all about listening to patients' stories and feelings, rather than just crunching numbers. It's the human side of nursing research!

question: Why should you stay right by the patient's side until they swallow their oral pills?

options.A: To clean up the empty plastic medication cup immediately
options.B: To engage in friendly conversation and build a strong therapeutic bond
options.C: To ensure the patient actually takes the drug rather than hiding or discarding it
options.D: To make sure the patient drinks an entire pitcher of cold water

explanation: Leaving pills at the bedside can lead to missed doses or accidental ingestion by visiting children. Always watch them swallow!

question: A nurse manager sees that patient falls are increasing on the ward. What should they do first?

options.A: Suspend all nursing staff on duty immediately
options.B: Review incident reports and audit unit safety practices
options.C: Ignore the data because falls are common in hospitals
options.D: Give every patient a written academic test on mobility

explanation: Before jumping to conclusions, always look at the data and evaluate the root cause so you can fix the actual problem.

question: What happens to complement protein levels (such as C3 and C4) in the blood during active serum sickness?

options.A: They decrease
options.B: They disappear entirely
options.C: They remain completely normal
options.D: They increase

explanation: Think of complement proteins as fuel used up in a fire; because the immune reaction is working overtime, these levels drop in the blood.

question: Which organ in the body is the main workstation for breaking down most medications?

options.A: The stomach
options.B: The kidneys
options.C: The liver
options.D: The pancreas

explanation: The liver is like the body's chemical factory. It uses special enzymes (the famous cytochrome P450 system) to process and break down most of the drugs we take.

question: When a nurse calls someone to let them know they were exposed to an illness, what must they NOT do?

options.A: Revealing the specific name and diagnosis of the index patient
options.B: Informing them that they spent time near someone with an infection
options.C: Explaining the symptoms to watch out for during the next two weeks
options.D: Giving instructions on how to access local testing and screening centers

explanation: Patient privacy is sacred! We can warn a contact that they were exposed without ever giving away the name of the original patient.

question: As a nurse, which vital signs must you always check before giving antianginal medications?

options.A: Oxygen saturation and pain scale
options.B: Height and weight measurements
options.C: Respiratory rate and temperature
options.D: Blood pressure and heart rate

explanation: Because these medications directly lower blood pressure and slow the heart, checking these vitals first keeps your patient safe from dangerous drops.

question: Why is it crucial to give quick feedback to staff after they submit an incident report?

options.A: It fulfills mandatory legal requirements for hospital tax exemptions
options.B: It stops patients from filing lawsuits against the medical facility
options.C: It shows staff that reporting leads to real system fixes rather than silence
options.D: It ensures that the nurse who made the mistake gets publicly reprimanded

explanation: When staff see their reports fix problems, they trust the system and keep speaking up to keep everyone safe.

question: Why do many patients forget to mention their herbal supplements during a medication history interview?

options.A: Herbal products dissolve instantly and leave no trace in the body
options.B: Hospital regulations strictly forbid talking about traditional medicine
options.C: Nurses never ask about home remedies during admission
options.D: They consider supplements to be harmless food items rather than real drugs

explanation: Patients often view herbs as 'just food' or natural, so it doesn't cross their minds to report them as medications. That's why we always have to ask!

question: You want to score how well nursing students perform sterile wound dressings in simulation. Which tool fits best?

options.A: An open-ended diary for students to write about their feelings
options.B: A simple task checklist that only records yes or no without scoring
options.C: A demographic questionnaire about the students' previous degrees
options.D: An evaluation or rating checklist to score the quality of performance

explanation: A rating checklist lets you assess how *well* a skill was done, going beyond a simple yes-or-no tick.

question: What is the primary focus of pharmacogenetics?

options.A: How genetic differences affect drug responses
options.B: How manufacturing plants create generic drugs
options.C: How bacteria develop resistance to antibiotics
options.D: How the human body excretes dietary proteins

explanation: Pharmacogenetics specifically studies how a person's inherited genetic makeup alters the way their body handles and responds to medications. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T5#GNS125_U1_T5_h1)

question: A nursing lecturer uses a physical heart model to explain blood flow to students with different learning styles. Which group benefits most from handling and examining this model directly?

options.A: Auditory learners
options.B: Kinesthetic learners
options.C: Visual learners
options.D: Reading learners

explanation: Kinesthetic learners learn best by touching, moving, and interacting physically with materials and models during a demonstration. [learn more](GST321_U8_T4#GST321_U8_T4_h2)

question: How do clinical audits and case reviews help improve healthcare delivery in a PAC unit?

options.A: By identifying system weaknesses and learning from them to prevent future errors
options.B: By creating strict rules that punish nurses for asking questions
options.C: By increasing the waiting time for patients arriving at the emergency room
options.D: By replacing all doctors and nurses with automated computer software

explanation: Good case reviews focus on fixing teamwork and hospital systems rather than pointing fingers, creating a much safer environment for both patients and staff.

question: Which type of medical mistake happens most often in hospitals?

options.A: Anesthesia overdoses
options.B: Wrong-site surgeries
options.C: Retained surgical instruments
options.D: Medication errors

explanation: Right! Giving the wrong drug, dose, or time is sadly the most common safety hiccup in healthcare. It's why we always double-check our rights of medication!

question: What is a primary benefit of patient support groups in primary health care?

options.A: They completely replace the need for professional medical checkups
options.B: They allow nurses to stop providing direct patient education
options.C: They serve as a revenue-generating business for the health clinic
options.D: They help patients feel less isolated and improve treatment adherence

explanation: Support groups offer peer encouragement, making patients more likely to stick to their medications and lifestyle changes. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T13#GNS124_U5_T13_h6)

question: A patient on combined pills reports mild nausea and tender breasts during her first week. What should you tell her?

options.A: Recommend immediate emergency surgery to check for blood clots
options.B: Reassure her that these are common mild adjustment side effects
options.C: Tell her to double her daily dose to help her body adjust faster
options.D: Instruct her to stop taking all medication immediately and report to the doctor

explanation: Take a breath—minor side effects are totally normal when starting estrogen as the body gets used to the new hormone levels. They usually clear up after a cycle or two!

question: What is the main goal of Human Resource Management (HRM) in a hospital?

options.A: Determining the hospital financial budget for the year
options.B: Repairing and maintaining hospital medical equipment
options.C: Managing staff from recruitment to retirement
options.D: Purchasing drugs and medical supplies for the pharmacy

explanation: Think of HR as the backbone for the people side of healthcare! HRM takes care of staff members right from when they apply for a job all the way to when they retire.

question: What bad thing can happen when an operating room has a harsh, strict, and intimidating atmosphere?

options.A: Management will cancel all safety meetings for good
options.B: Patients will magically stop getting wound infections
options.C: Junior staff may be too scared to speak up about safety mistakes
options.D: Surgeons will finish every single surgery twice as fast

explanation: When people are afraid of being shouted at or humiliated, they stay quiet about errors. Teamwork and patient safety require an environment where everyone can speak freely.

question: What is the main reason for running routine daily or weekly self-tests on an AED?

options.A: Transmit patient data logs directly to local emergency dispatchers
options.B: Ensure the device is functional and ready for an emergency
options.C: Calibrate the internal software to match local voltage standards
options.D: Recharge the internal lithium battery without manual plug-in

explanation: Routine self-tests check the battery and circuitry so you can rest easy knowing the machine won't fail when a real emergency happens.

question: Why are bedside nurses so great at leading quality improvement?

options.A: They are the only ones who understand data statistics
options.B: They handle the hospital's financial budgets
options.C: They spend their time sitting in administrative offices
options.D: They see daily workflow issues and safety risks firsthand

explanation: Spot on! Because you're right there at the bedside delivering care every day, you know better than anyone where things slow down or break. Your daily experience is a superpower!

question: Why should you call or alert the receiving hospital before the patient physically arrives?

options.A: To allow the specialist team time to prepare necessary equipment and space
options.B: To prevent the patient from changing their mind during transit
options.C: To give the nurse permission to leave the clinic early
options.D: To ensure the hospital bed fee is paid in advance by mobile money

explanation: Spot on! Calling ahead gives the emergency or specialist team precious time to ready their staff, drugs, and equipment before the patient rolls in.

question: Which snail-shaped structure in the inner ear handles hearing?

options.A: Cochlea
options.B: Semicircular canals
options.C: Eustachian tube
options.D: Auricle

explanation: Spot on! The cochlea is packed with fluid and tiny cells that turn sound vibrations into messages your brain can understand.

question: Why are community-based approaches important alongside clinic visits?

options.A: They allow nurses to fine men who refuse to visit the clinic.
options.B: They replace the need for any hospitals or clinics in rural areas.
options.C: They reach men within their own social environments and cultural comfort zones.
options.D: They ensure that women stay indoors during pregnancy.

explanation: Taking health talks to town halls and local spots engages men right where they naturally gather. Fantastic job!

question: How should a nurse properly perform a whisper test to check a patient's hearing?

options.A: Inspect the deep ear canal with an otoscope to check for active infection
options.B: Whisper numbers and letters while standing slightly behind the patient
options.C: Shout loudly from across the room to test maximum volume tolerance
options.D: Use a tuning fork directly placed on the center of the patient's forehead

explanation: You got it! Standing behind them stops them from reading your lips, giving you an accurate test for each ear on its own.

question: What does emotional intelligence mainly mean for a nurse leader?

options.A: Memorizing every institutional policy word for word
options.B: Understanding and managing one's own emotions while empathizing with others
options.C: Suppressing all personal feelings to maintain a strict professional exterior
options.D: Using rapid mathematical calculations to manage unit budgets

explanation: Emotional intelligence is all about self-awareness and empathy—knowing how you feel and genuinely connecting with your team's feelings too.

question: Which bone shape category does the patella ( kneecap) belong to?

options.A: Flat bone
options.B: Irregular bone
options.C: Long bone
options.D: Sesamoid bone

explanation: Sesamoid bones like the patella develop inside tendons to protect them from excessive wear and tear. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T4#GNS121_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which of these best describes an environmental reservoir for a disease germ?

options.A: A mosquito biting a person with malaria
options.B: An asymptomatic person carrying typhoid
options.C: A nurse caring for an infected child
options.D: Soil containing tetanus spores

explanation: Soil, water, and air can act as environmental reservoirs where germs live naturally outside of a human body.

question: Why do modern nursing guidelines usually discourage using traditional circular air rings (doughnut cushions)?

options.A: The rim can cut off blood flow and worsen tissue damage
options.B: They are too expensive to clean and disinfect between patients
options.C: They make it impossible to adjust the hospital bed height
options.D: They trap excessive moisture and cause fungal infections

explanation: That's right! The hard edges of a doughnut cushion squeeze surrounding tiny blood vessels, cutting off circulation and actually increasing the risk of pressure sores.

question: A patient says they cannot afford the expensive imported supplements prescribed elsewhere. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Report the patient to the hospital management
options.B: Tell the patient to stop eating altogether
options.C: Tell them to borrow money to buy the brand
options.D: Help the patient find affordable local whole-food alternatives

explanation: Brilliant! As a nurse, you bridge the gap by showing patients how to get great nutrition using what is easily available around them.

question: You want to improve child health in a rural village. What is the best first step?

options.A: Distribute standard vitamins without checking local diets
options.B: Ask local mothers about their main health concerns
options.C: Build a modern pediatric ward immediately
options.D: Report village leaders to the ministry of health

explanation: Brilliant! Talking directly to the community helps you understand their real challenges instead of just guessing what they need.

question: Which dangerous practice with used needles should every nurse avoid completely?

options.A: Carrying sharps boxes on a trolley
options.B: Dropping syringes into yellow bins
options.C: Recapping used needles by hand
options.D: Checking fill lines on containers

explanation: Never try to recap a needle with your hands! It's one of the leading causes of accidental needle-stick injuries in nursing.

question: In healthcare quality improvement, what does "spreading" an idea mean?

options.A: Spreading a contagious disease from one patient room to another
options.B: Expanding the physical size of the hospital emergency department
options.C: Increasing the total number of nursing staff on every hospital shift
options.D: Taking a successful local change and sharing it with other units or facilities

explanation: You've got this! Spread simply means taking a great idea that worked well in one ward and sharing it so other care areas can benefit too.

question: Which of these is NOT a warning sign of a pelvic infection after a procedure?

options.A: Foul-smelling or purulent vaginal discharge
options.B: Severe and worsening lower abdominal pain
options.C: Persistent fever and chills
options.D: Sudden development of normal morning appetite

explanation: Spot on! Wanting to eat normally is a sign of a happy, healing body. Fever, bad-smelling discharge, and terrible pain are the real warning signs to watch out for.

question: Where does fertilization of the human egg normally happen?

options.A: In the ampulla of the fallopian tube
options.B: Along the lower third of the myometrium
options.C: Directly inside the uterine cavity
options.D: Within the peritoneal cavity of the pelvis

explanation: Spot on! The sperm and egg usually meet in the widest part of the fallopian tube, called the ampulla, before starting their trip to the uterus. You've got this!

question: Why did clinical research take a backseat to educational studies in early nursing history?

options.A: Nursing was heavily focused on following fixed hospital routines and administrative tasks
options.B: Physicians refused to let nurses learn how to read write research papers
options.C: There were no sick patients available in hospitals for students to study
options.D: Government laws strictly forbade nurses from observing patient symptoms

explanation: Great job thinking this through! Back then, nursing was driven more by strict hospital traditions and routines than by independent science, so administrative duties came first.

question: Why are deep breathing exercises so important for a patient stuck on bed rest in traction?

options.A: They relax tight muscles to stop spasms
options.B: They stimulate blood flow inside the deep calf veins
options.C: They expand the lungs fully to prevent mucus buildup and collapse
options.D: They increase the pulling force of the traction weights

explanation: Thinking like a real nurse! Lying in bed slows down breathing, which can cause lung issues. Deep breaths keep the tiny air sacs open and clear out mucus.

question: A patient suddenly loses the pulse in their right foot, and the limb becomes cold, pale, and very painful. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: A sudden blood clot blocking an artery (acute arterial occlusion)
options.B: Raynaud's phenomenon triggered by stress
options.C: Superficial vein inflammation in the calf
options.D: Chronic venous swelling with mild fluid retention

explanation: When an artery gets suddenly blocked, blood can't get down to the foot at all. This is an emergency marked by the famous 'P' signs: pain, pallor, pulselessness, and coldness!

question: What resource problem often leads to unsafe injection practices in underfunded clinics?

options.A: Excessive supplies of single-use packaging
options.B: Severe shortages of sterile needles and syringes
options.C: An excess of trained supervisory personnel
options.D: Too many mandatory safety meetings

explanation: Spot on. When a facility runs out of basic gear, stressed workers are put in tough spots where maintaining safety becomes a struggle.

question: Which quick screening tool do healthcare workers use to check for problem drinking?

options.A: Braden scale
options.B: Apgar score chart
options.C: CAGE questionnaire
options.D: Glasgow Coma Scale

explanation: The CAGE questionnaire is a short, simple set of four questions used to spot lifetime alcohol problems. Easy to remember!

question: Why are finger foods so helpful for patients with advanced dementia during meals?

options.A: It prevents the patient from spilling liquids on their hospital gown
options.B: It guarantees the patient will eat three full meals every single day
options.C: It promotes independence and makes eating easier for confused patients
options.D: It eliminates the need for any nursing staff supervision

explanation: Spot on! When handling cutlery gets confusing, finger foods let patients feed themselves and hold onto their dignity.

question: What is a major danger of having bad sanitation and broken toilets in a school?

options.A: Rapid spread of infectious diseases like cholera
options.B: Immediate decline in mathematical reasoning skills
options.C: Permanent loss of hearing acuity in students
options.D: Sudden increase in genetic disorders among pupils

explanation: Correct! Dirty surroundings and unsafe water easily lead to water-borne illnesses and tummy infections among children.

question: Which suture separates the forehead bone (frontal bone) from the two top side bones (parietal bones)?

options.A: Sagittal suture
options.B: Coronal suture
options.C: Lambdoid suture
options.D: Metopic suture

explanation: You've got this! The coronal suture runs side to side across the skull like a crown, sitting right between the frontal and parietal bones.

question: Which nutrient class serves as the body's most rapid and preferred energy source?

options.A: Vitamins
options.B: Carbohydrates
options.C: Minerals
options.D: Proteins

explanation: Carbohydrates break down quickly into glucose, which is the body and brain's favorite fuel for immediate energy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T001#GNS227_U2_T001_h2)

question: Why do doctors still order lab tests even when a male patient's physical symptoms look obvious?

options.A: Hospitals require blood tests for insurance billing purposes
options.B: Different STIs can present with very similar clinical signs
options.C: Antibiotics will not work without a written laboratory report
options.D: Physical exams cannot detect any form of genital infection

explanation: Many STIs look identical on the outside (like causing the same discharge or sores). Lab tests tell us the exact germ so we use the right drug.

question: Which of these is an actual 'system-level' fix to improve patient safety?

options.A: Redesigning electronic medication screens to make high-risk doses harder to select
options.B: Warning all nursing staff to pay closer attention during their shifts
options.C: Posting a memo on the staff bulletin board about being careful
options.D: Suspending the nurse involved in the error for a period of two weeks

explanation: That's a true system fix! Changing how a computer system or tool works makes doing the right thing much easier and mistakes much harder to make.

question: Why might a woman with Type III FGM need a procedure called defibulation during childbirth?

options.A: To prevent severe postpartum hemorrhage from the uterus
options.B: To allow the baby to pass through the narrowed vaginal opening
options.C: To correct an underlying urinary tract infection
options.D: To speed up the delivery of the placenta

explanation: Spot on! The scar tissue seal blocks the birth canal, so healthcare providers must surgically open the area during labor to keep mother and baby safe.

question: Why do you need to understand how the lymphatic system drains the reproductive organs?

options.A: It explains how menstrual cramps travel down to the legs
options.B: It shows how vaginal pH changes during a bacterial infection
options.C: It dictates the correct dosage for oral contraceptive pills
options.D: It helps track how pelvic cancers can spread through the body

explanation: Exactly! Cancer cells can hitch a ride through lymph vessels to nearby lymph nodes, so knowing these pathways is super important for staging and treatment.

question: Which professional group takes the lead in finding safe shelter and tracing families for a rescued child?

options.A: Social workers
options.B: Hospital pharmacists
options.C: Laboratory scientists
options.D: Surgical technicians

explanation: Social workers are experts in child protection, welfare placements, and finding safe homes or foster care.
